steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal entered: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030, with an $800,000 capital budget (2027 budget year).
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Standard efficiency work alone (no solar) is estimated to cut about 6.2% to 17.6% of annual grid electricity, which does not reach the 30% goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Standard efficiency plus rooftop solar, sized to fit the budget, is estimated to cut about 28.3% to 41.9% of annual use. The low end is just under 30%, so this option does not reliably reach the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Deeper efficiency, solar on the whole usable roof and a backup battery is estimated to cut about 31.4% to 46.3% of annual use, so it reaches the goal even at the low end. Its upfront cost may be up to $306,329 more than the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Rooftop solar alone is only about 22% to 24% of annual use and does not reach the 30% goal by itself.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Meeting the goal may take more than the $800,000 set aside. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision once the gap is compared with the estimated savings.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: P.S. 236 Langston Hughes (Department of Education building X173), an elementary school at 1871 Walton Avenue, Bronx, built in 1994, with 46,700 sq ft of floor area as entered, a flat roof of 10,260 sq ft as entered, served by Con Edison.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: No existing solar, other renewables or efficiency work were entered, so the plan assumes none exist. The goal baseline is the electricity the building buys from the grid.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Annual grid electricity of 456,834 kWh (kWh is energy over time) matches the city's Local Law 84 energy report for 2024. This figure is the baseline.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's tax lot record (tax lot number 2028510021) is listed under 1869 Walton Avenue, not 1871. It may be another frontage or door number of the same lot. It shows 46,700 sq ft gross floor area, 4 floors and no landmark flag.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's building footprints show one building with about 10,255 sq ft of ground area, close to the 10,260 sq ft roof area entered. A footprint is ground area, not a measured roof.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The Local Law 84 report lists the school at 43,760 sq ft, site EUI (energy use per square foot) of 57.6 kBtu (thousand BTU) per sq ft and an Energy Star score of 69.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output is given as a range from system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the standard 14% assumption; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof is taken as 55% of the roof area, to leave room for edges, equipment and walkways.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: About 66 sq ft of usable roof is needed per kW (how much power at one moment) of solar panels.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Critical load was not given, so it is estimated at 1.0 watt per sq ft x 46,700 sq ft = 46.7 kW (a planning estimate, not metered). Backup length was not given, so 8 hours is assumed. Battery energy = kW x hours / 0.85 round-trip efficiency = 440 kWh.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED lighting and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Prices are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes: solar $3,131-4,668 per kW, battery $546-812 per kWh, and efficiency $1.17-4.02 per kWh saved per year (standard) or $1.09-3.83 (deep), each the middle half of completed NYC projects (NYSERDA data). Efficiency savings of 10-20% (standard) and 15-25% (deep) are planning estimates, and only 62%-88% of them is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report, FY2022).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Baseline is 456,834 kWh a year of electricity bought from the grid, taken from the city's 2024 energy report and matching the entered figure.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A standard efficiency package (LED lighting and building controls) is estimated to save about 28,324 to 80,403 kWh a year after counting only the share the City's audited projects delivered (62%-88% of predicted savings). The underlying 10-20% is a planning estimate.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The intake did not say what lighting, controls or cooling the school has. If LED lighting or controls are already installed, the savings and confidence are lower, and those measures should not be repeated.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The deeper efficiency package used in the full path is estimated to save about 15-25% before the 62%-88% share is applied.
claims.label: ESTIMATE
claims.units: % of annual use before realization trim

claims.text: Usable roof is about 5,643 sq ft from the 10,260 sq ft roof entered.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The usable roof fits an array of about 85.5 kW DC.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Estimated solar output is about 101,100 to 111,098 kWh a year, with a central value of about 106,101 kWh. The range comes from the assumed loss band of 18% to 10%.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: That central output is about 23% of annual use, so solar alone does not reach the 30% goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Solar bill savings are about $20,028 to $26,864 a year, using the low output with the low price ($0.1981 per kWh) and the high output with the high price ($0.2418 per kWh). The price is the New York commercial average, not this building's own tariff.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The city's Local Law 24 assessment rates this roof Not Solar Ready, with a roof age of 20 years or more and a condition of Fair. The roof should be checked, and possibly repaired or replaced, before solar. The roof area and usable share should also be verified by an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario A (standard efficiency only): reduction of about 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, or 21% to 59% of the goal. It does not reach the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario A: typical upfront cost range is $80,174 to $275,471 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $175,424). Counted incentives are $0, so net cost is the same. Simple payback is about 4.1 to 49.1 years. The cost fits within the budget. No backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B (standard efficiency plus solar within budget): reduction of about 28.3% to 41.9% of annual use, or 94% to 140% of the goal. It does not reach the goal at the low end.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B: typical upfront range is $347,875 to $674,585 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $487,585). Net cost after the federal credit is about $267,565 to $554,851. Simple payback is about 5.8 to 21.6 years. The cost fits within the budget. No backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C (deep efficiency, whole usable roof of solar and a backup battery): reduction of about 31.4% to 46.3% of annual use, or 105% to 154% of the goal. It reaches the goal even at the low end.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C: typical upfront range is $607,530 to $1,106,329 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $841,944). Net cost after the federal credit is about $455,148 to $879,411. Simple payback is about 8.9 to 30.9 years. Budget strain: may exceed budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C costs up to $306,329 more than your budget. It reaches the goal, but reaching it may take more than the amount set aside. Compare that gap with the savings before deciding whether to extend the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Backup outage hours: Scenario C is estimated to carry the critical loads for about 8 to 9.4 hours. Scenarios A and B give no backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Payback here is a simple payback, not a full financial model. The $800,000 capital budget is treated as one total upfront figure. The roof could not produce more than the school uses, so no surplus solar arises.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The heating fuel is outside an electricity goal: the city's energy report shows natural gas (893,000 kBtu) and fuel oil (69,276 kBtu) use, which these scenarios do not reduce.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario C, deeper efficiency line: the expanded efficiency package has a typical range of $99,590 to $349,935 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $227,503), based on 91,367 kWh saved a year at $1.09-3.83 per kWh saved from completed NYC public-sector projects (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, rooftop solar line: typical range $267,700 to $399,114 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $312,160), from 85.5 kW at $3,131-4,668 per kW, the middle half of 558 completed NYC non-residential projects of 25-100 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, backup battery line: typical range $240,240 to $357,280 (the median of similar NYC projects is about $302,280), from 440 kWh at $546-812 per kWh, the middle half of 56 completed or approved NYC storage projects (NYSERDA data). The battery is the largest single cost that is not needed for the 30% goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, federal credit line: the credit is counted as $152,382 to $226,918 off (30% of solar and battery), but only because the program page shows it open. The program page says whether this school qualifies is not confirmed, and the solar must be placed in service by December 31, 2027. Retrieved October 19, 2026.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, itemized: standard efficiency $80,174 to $275,471 (median about $175,424); rooftop solar $267,700 to $399,114 (median about $312,160); federal credit of $80,310 to $119,734 off. Typical upfront is $347,875 to $674,585 before the credit.

claims.text: Federal elective pay (direct pay) for governmental entities is open per the IRS page, with a deadline of December 31, 2027 for solar placed in service. It is counted in net cost above; if the school does not qualify or misses the date, net cost is the upfront range instead.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The NYC Solar Schools program (DCAS, NYPA and NYC Public Schools, solar under power purchase agreements) is uncertain: the city's release describes no enrollment process and it is not known whether this school is in the pipeline. It is left out of net cost.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The NYSERDA NY-Sun commercial solar incentive is uncertain: the current incentive block status could not be read from an official page by a program. It is left out of net cost until checked in a browser.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: confirm the 12-month bills, the 2027 capital budget and whether it can be extended, the building's own tariff (savings here use the New York average price), and the roof replacement year.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed professional engineer (PE) or registered architect (RA) for the structural analysis, plus a roof condition survey and a roofer's quote, before any solar design.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: LED lighting and building controls where not already installed, and other measures from an energy audit, first because they are the lowest-cost path.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and interconnection: Department of Buildings permits, a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, and the Con Edison interconnection application. Ask DCAS or the SCA about the Solar Schools program at the same time.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation: an array of up to about 85.5 kW on the usable roof, after the roof is judged sound, with timing set against the December 2027 in-service date for the federal credit.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: add the backup battery if the budget is extended, then compare actual electricity bills with the estimates after the first year.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how the school can cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 on an $800,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that the full path (deeper efficiency work, solar on the whole usable roof and a backup battery) cuts about 31% to 46% of grid electricity, so it reaches the goal even at the cautious end. It costs about $607,530 to $1,106,329 upfront, up to $306,329 more than your budget. The version that fits the budget (standard efficiency plus rooftop solar) reaches about 28% to 42%, so it may fall just short. Rooftop solar alone covers only about 22% to 24% of your use. The building has no solar or efficiency work already, and the figure counts electricity bought from the grid. The city rates the roof not solar ready and 20 years old or more, and none of the costs include roof repair or replacement. Next: have a roofer and a licensed engineer assess the roof, then ask the Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS) or the School Construction Authority (SCA) about the Solar Schools program before deciding whether to extend the budget.
